label: 计算机体系结构与性能模型

questions.learningObjective: Apply the Roofline model to classify a batch-1 GEMV as compute- or memory-bound on a specific GPU and derive the achievable throughput ceiling from arithmetic intensity times HBM bandwidth.
questions.stem: On A100 SXM (peak FP16 Tensor-Core throughput ≈ 312 TFLOP/s, HBM2e bandwidth ≈ 2.0 TB/s), consider a batch-1 GEMV y = W x with W ∈ ℝ^{4096×4096} FP16, x ∈ ℝ^{4096} FP16, y ∈ ℝ^{4096} FP16 (all resident in HBM, weights streamed once, negligible reuse). Assuming steady state and ignoring launch overhead, which Roofline characterization is correct?

options.text: Compute-bound; the achievable ceiling is approximately the FP16 Tensor-Core peak of about 312 TFLOP/s, since Tensor Cores are the dispatched math path for FP16 GEMV kernels on A100.
Compute-bound; the operational intensity for this GEMV is ≈ 2 FLOP/byte, comfortably above the A100 FP32 ridge point (~ 9.75 FLOP/byte), so the SMs saturate at the FP32 peak of 19.5 TFLOP/s.
Memory-bound; AI ≈ 1 FLOP/byte is far below A100's FP16 ridge point (~ 153 FLOP/byte), so the ceiling is HBM × AI ≈ 2 TFLOP/s.
Memory-bound, but the binding ceiling is set by on-chip shared-memory (SRAM) bandwidth rather than HBM, because Tensor-Core GEMV routes each weight through SMEM staging before consumption.

assumptions: Weights resident in HBM, no persistent-kernel weight caching.
Launch and kernel-overhead time excluded from steady-state analysis.

questions.learningObjective: Given an elementwise kernel's per-element FLOP and byte cost, compute the arithmetic intensity and classify the kernel against a specific GPU's FP32 ridge point.
questions.stem: On A100 SXM (peak FP32 ≈ 19.5 TFLOP/s, HBM ≈ 2.0 TB/s), a kernel reads an FP32 tensor A of shape [32M] and writes B[i] = softplus(A[i]) (≈ 10 FLOPs per element). Which Roofline analysis is correct?

options.text: Compute-bound; the 10 FLOPs per element push arithmetic intensity above the FP32 ridge point, so the achievable ceiling is close to the A100 FP32 peak of 19.5 TFLOP/s.
Memory-bound; arithmetic intensity ≈ 2.5 FLOP/byte, obtained by counting only the input reads and ignoring the output writes since writes are asynchronous on the memory bus.
Memory-bound; AI = 10/8 = 1.25 FLOP/byte < A100 FP32 ridge (~ 9.75); ceiling ≈ 2.5 TFLOP/s.
Compute-bound; achievable throughput ≈ 19.5 TFLOP/s because element-wise kernels always saturate the SM math pipelines once occupancy exceeds 50%.

assumptions: No cache reuse: each byte of A is read from HBM exactly once, each byte of B is written to HBM exactly once.
Softplus operates on a single tensor and does not fuse with adjacent ops in this measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Apply Little's Law to compute the number of in-flight memory loads required to saturate a GPU's HBM bandwidth given a target latency.
questions.stem: Little's Law states Concurrency = Bandwidth × Latency. Suppose an A100 has peak HBM bandwidth ≈ 2 TB/s and average DRAM load latency ≈ 400 ns, and each in-flight load fetches a 128-byte sector. Approximately how many 128-byte loads must be simultaneously in flight (aggregated across all SMs) to saturate HBM bandwidth?

options.text: ≈ 32 concurrent loads — one per warp scheduler on a single SM — because Little's Law counts per-scheduler concurrency, not aggregate outstanding requests across all SMs.
≈ 400 loads (roughly one per SM times four schedulers, since A100 has ~ 108 SMs and each SM has four warp schedulers dispatching one load at a time in steady state).
The number is independent of latency; only bandwidth determines the required concurrency, since bandwidth by itself already characterizes the memory system's throughput ceiling.

assumptions: DRAM latency and bandwidth are steady-state, aggregate figures for the GPU.
Each load request completes in ~ 400 ns on average.
Requests are for 128-byte sectors (typical L2 sector granularity for coalesced accesses).

questions.subtopic: GPU memory hierarchy / bandwidth / access rules
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish structural and access-pattern properties of NVIDIA GPU memory tiers (register file, shared memory, constant memory, global memory).
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the A100 (sm_80) memory hierarchy are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The per-SM register file (65,536 × 32-bit ≈ 256 KB) is larger than the per-SM configurable L1/shared-memory partition (up to 192 KB total on A100).

Aggregate global-memory (HBM2e) bandwidth on the A100 board is higher than the aggregate on-chip shared-memory bandwidth summed across all SMs, since HBM stacks scale linearly with pin count and channels.

Shared memory is bank-organized: warp threads accessing distinct addresses in the same bank serialize (bank conflict); global memory has no banks but obeys coalescing rules on 32/64/128 B transactions.
Constant memory accesses in which all threads of a warp read the same address are broadcast, avoiding a per-thread memory transaction and delivering the value in one cycle to the whole warp.

assumptions: Shared-memory bank width = 32-bit (4 bytes) per bank.

questions.learningObjective: From ptxas register report and launch configuration, derive the register-file-limited theoretical occupancy on a given GPU architecture.
questions.stem: A CUDA kernel targeting sm_80 is compiled with `nvcc -arch=sm_80 --ptxas-options=-v` and prints `ptxas info : Used 96 registers, 384 bytes cmem[0]`. The launch config is `<<<gridDim, 256>>>`. A100 provides 65,536 32-bit registers per SM, a max of 2,048 threads (64 warps) per SM, and up to 32 concurrent blocks per SM. Ignoring shared-memory and block-count limits, what is the register-limited theoretical occupancy?
questions.profileData: Used 96 registers, 384 bytes cmem[0]; block size = 256; per-SM: 65536 regs, max 2048 threads (64 warps), max 32 blocks

options.text: 50% (32 of 64 warps active per SM); 96 registers per thread and 256 threads per block allow 4 concurrent blocks per SM under the register-file budget.
100%; A100's register file is large enough to accommodate 8 concurrent blocks of 256 threads at 96 registers per thread, so occupancy hits the SM's maximum of 64 warps.
12.5%; the effective limit is 8 concurrent blocks per SM regardless of register usage, since Ampere caps blocks-per-SM at 8 rather than 32 in practice.

assumptions: Shared memory usage per block is small enough to not further limit occupancy.
Grid dimension is large enough to fully populate the SMs (not launch-limited).
